facts.text: Rasputin was born into a Siberian peasant family and eventually gained extraordinary access to the Russian imperial family.
He became particularly important to Empress Alexandra because she believed he could help her son Alexei during attacks of hemophilia.
Despite the nickname 'Mad Monk,' Rasputin was never actually an ordained Russian Orthodox monk.
His drinking, womanizing, and relationships with admirers helped make him one of the most scandalous figures in late Imperial Russia.
Rasputin was assassinated in 1916 by conspirators that included Prince Felix Yusupov and Grand Duke Dmitri Pavlovich.
The famous story says Rasputin survived cyanide, beatings, and gunshots before finally drowning beneath an icy river. It is a fantastic story, but much of it probably did not happen.
The autopsy reportedly found no poison in Rasputin's body, seriously undermining the famous poisoned-cakes portion of his murder story.
Enemies circulated claims that Rasputin was secretly having an affair with Empress Alexandra. Historians have found no convincing evidence for it.
Rasputin's reputation for supernatural healing became enormous, although more mundane explanations have been proposed for why Alexei sometimes improved under his care.
Tycho lost part of his nose in a sword duel with another Danish nobleman after an argument over mathematics.
He wore a prosthetic nose afterward. Although legend often calls it gold or silver, analysis of his remains suggests the everyday prosthesis was probably brass.
Before the telescope existed, Tycho made astronomical observations precise enough to become essential evidence for later models of the Solar System.
Tycho's observations of a new star in 1572 helped undermine the old idea that the heavens beyond the Moon were eternally unchanging.
Johannes Kepler gained access to Tycho's extraordinarily precise observations after Tycho's death and used them in developing his laws of planetary motion.
Tycho reportedly kept a tame elk at his estate.

According to an early biographical account, Tycho's elk was visiting another nobleman's house, drank a great deal of beer, fell down a staircase, and died. History occasionally refuses to be improved upon.
Tycho also kept a man named Jepp as a court jester and reportedly believed that Jepp possessed clairvoyant abilities.

For centuries a popular story claimed Tycho died because court etiquette prevented him from leaving a banquet to urinate. Modern examination has weakened both the ruptured-bladder story and theories that he was poisoned.

Ada's father, Lord Byron, once acquired a tame bear while attending Trinity College because the rules prohibited keeping dogs but apparently neglected to prohibit bears. When questioned about it, Byron joked that the bear should sit for a college fellowship.
Ada was the only legitimate child of the poet Lord Byron.
Her parents separated shortly after her birth, and Ada never developed a relationship with Byron.
Her mother deliberately encouraged mathematics and logic in Ada's education, partly out of fear that she might inherit Byron's temperament.
While writing about Charles Babbage's Analytical Engine, Ada described an algorithm for calculating Bernoulli numbers and is consequently often described as the first computer programmer.
Ada understood something remarkably modern about computing: she realized a sufficiently capable machine might manipulate symbols representing things other than numbers, including music.
Ada became heavily involved in gambling on horse races and attempted to apply mathematical thinking to betting.
Her gambling went badly enough to leave her thousands of pounds in debt.
Stories later claimed Ada lost enormous fortunes and repeatedly pawned the family jewels. Some versions appear considerably more dramatic than the surviving evidence supports.
Ada was surrounded by rumors of extramarital affairs. The surviving evidence leaves parts of her private life frustratingly ambiguous.
Charles Dickens visited Ada while she was dying and, at her request, read to her from Dombey and Son.
Crowley was an occultist, ceremonial magician, writer, poet, painter, and unusually accomplished mountaineer.
He participated in the pioneering 1902 expedition attempting K2, decades before the mountain was successfully climbed.
Crowley later led a disastrous 1905 attempt on Kangchenjunga, during which members of the expedition rebelled against his leadership.
Several members of the Kangchenjunga expedition were killed in an avalanche while descending after Crowley warned them that continuing downward was dangerous.
Crowley founded the religion and philosophy of Thelema, whose best-known maxim begins 'Do what thou wilt.'
British newspapers famously branded Crowley 'the wickedest man in the world,' a reputation he did little to discourage.
Crowley deliberately cultivated scandal and provocation, making the boundary between his genuine beliefs and his public persona unusually difficult to untangle.
He experimented extensively with drugs and wrote openly about his experiences at a time when doing so was especially scandalous.

Crowley's activities during World War I generated persistent claims that he was secretly working for British intelligence while publicly writing anti-British propaganda in the United States. His exact relationship with intelligence services remains debated.

Many sensational stories about Crowley involve satanism, human sacrifice, or supernatural crimes. His actual life was strange enough that these inventions should not be confused with documented history.
Marie Curie was the first woman to receive a Nobel Prize.
She became the first person ever awarded two Nobel Prizes and remains the only person to win Nobels in two different scientific fields: Physics and Chemistry.
Marie and Pierre Curie's research led to the discovery of polonium and radium.
Polonium was named for Poland, Marie's homeland, which at the time did not exist as an independent country.
During World War I, Curie organized mobile X-ray units that could be brought near the battlefield to help surgeons locate bullets and fractures.
After Pierre Curie's death, Marie took over his professorship and became the first female professor at the University of Paris.
Curie's long exposure to radioactive material occurred before its dangers were properly understood and contributed to the illness that eventually killed her.
In 1911, Curie's relationship with married physicist Paul Langevin became a major public scandal after private correspondence reached the press.
The scandal became so vicious that an angry crowd gathered outside Curie's home and she and her daughters sought refuge with friends.
Hostile newspapers falsely claimed Curie was Jewish and suggested that her relationship with Langevin had begun while Pierre was alive. The attacks mixed genuine scandal with xenophobic fabrication.
Decades later, Marie Curie's granddaughter Hélène married Paul Langevin's grandson Michel. History has a sense of humor.
Mary Mallon was an Irish-born cook who became the first person identified in the United States as an asymptomatic carrier of the bacteria responsible for typhoid fever.
Mallon herself did not show the symptoms that devastated people around her, which contributed to her refusal to believe that she was spreading the disease.
Sanitation engineer George Soper traced outbreaks among wealthy households to kitchens where Mallon had worked.
When Soper first confronted Mallon and requested blood, urine, and stool samples, she reacted angrily and refused.
New York health authorities forcibly quarantined Mallon on North Brother Island in 1907.
She was released in 1910 after agreeing not to work as a cook.
Mallon eventually returned to cooking and used assumed surnames, including Mary Brown.
After another typhoid outbreak was traced to a maternity hospital where she worked, Mallon was quarantined again and remained isolated for the rest of her life.
The exact number of infections and deaths attributable to Mallon varies between historical accounts. Claims should therefore be treated as estimates rather than a precise body count.

Mallon was not the only known healthy typhoid carrier. Her extraordinarily long confinement has since become part of a larger debate about public health, individual liberty, class, and the unequal treatment of disease carriers.
The nickname 'Typhoid Mary' outlived Mallon and became an expression for someone who spreads disease, largely erasing the actual person behind the phrase.
